Euclid I43

AreaGeometryTriangles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: pieces of the same colour on opposite sides of the slanted line always cover the same amount of space.
How to play: Drag the corners A, B, C and D, or the numbered dots on the line. Use the minus and plus buttons to choose up to ten dots, or focus a dot and press the arrow keys.
Look for the math

Move a point along the diagonal and the coloured pieces change shape, but each colour still covers exactly as much space on one side of the diagonal as on the other. That is the small, surprising fact behind a proposition written down over two thousand years ago.

One point on the diagonal

Start with one dot K on the diagonal AC. Through K the picture draws a line parallel to AB and another parallel to AD. They cut the parallelogram into one piece at A, one at C, and two green pieces facing each other across the diagonal. In the applet's own order those four fills are A G K E, G B F K, H D E K and F C H K. The page claims that pieces of the same colour on opposite sides have equal area: here Area(GBFK) = Area(HDEK). The logic test checks this on 250 shapes and dot positions, with the dot dragged freely along the diagonal; it holds every time.

Equal triangles, equal leftovers

Euclid's proof matches the triangles on the two sides: the page names AKH, KCF and ACD against KEA, CGK and CBA, equal by SSS or ASA. Take those equal triangles away from equal larger ones and the two green leftovers, called HKFD and EBGK on the page, must be equal even though their shapes differ. This is Proposition I.43 of Euclid's Elements; the argument is subtraction of congruent pieces, not a measurement.

Ten points, still equal

With two or more dots the parallel lines form a little grid. Each small rectangle in that grid is finally coloured by the last dot whose square covers it; the rectangle reflected across the diagonal is covered by exactly the same dot, so it gets the same colour and has the same area. The page says the statement stays true for any number of points and follows by repeating the one-point argument. The test searches all 140 combinations of every setting from 0 to 10 dots on many slanted shapes, including dragged dots: thousands of reflected pairs, all with matching colours and matching areas. The applet's spinner actually starts at 0, so an empty diagonal is included too, and the claim holds there in the only way it can: there are no pieces left to compare.

How this differs from the extension

This applet keeps every dot on the diagonal. The companion Euclid I.43 Extended page lets a single point X sit anywhere inside the parallelogram and builds an extra parallelogram XBYD, with points R, S, U, V, W, K, E and F, to make up the difference between the two areas; it also shows a second, same-side pair of equal areas. It credits Quang Tuan Bui for that extension. Here there is no construction and no off-diagonal point: the claim is only the original one, that same-coloured pieces on opposite sides of the diagonal match.

Try this: set ten dots, then drag the middle one. Two same-coloured pieces grow and shrink together, and the status line keeps calling the pairs equal.
